source_read: PDF, pp. 1493-1504 (born-digital text read in full; pp. 1495 and 1497-1503 checked on rendered pages at 150 dpi; equation 3 on p. 1496 and Figures 2-4 at 300 dpi)

claims.overstatement: The claim presents the model correctly as showing that the patterns cannot by themselves identify a cause, not as disproving a gateway effect. Minor points: (1) 'a strong relative risk of using heroin, cocaine or hallucinogens after cannabis': the relative risk compares hard-drug use by 21 between people who had and had not used cannabis by 21 (estimation, p. 1499; results, p. 1500); the model section speaks of 'prior' cannabis initiation, but the survey figure of 24 does not require cannabis to come first, so 'among people who had used cannabis by 21' is exact. (2) '11 per 1,000, against 16' is per 1,000 people, not per 1,000 who used both, and counts hard drugs as first only when at least a year before cannabis (same-year starts are not counted), as the magnitude says. (3) The model's propensity is defined as a propensity to report drug use, so systematic under-reporting could produce the same patterns (p. 1502); a qualifier the claim could carry, not an overstatement. (4) Added after step 2 (the card's reporting issue 4, checked against pp. 1501-1502): what the paper calls the reliability of the propensity indicator is the correlation between indicator and propensity (a reliability of 0.99 is said to leave 2% of the variance uncaptured, and the text speaks of a 0.99 correlation), so the magnitude's 'liability measure of reliability 0.8' is an indicator correlated 0.8 with the liability, capturing 64% of its variance; on the usual definition its reliability is 0.64. Suggested wording: 'a liability measure correlated 0.8 with the liability (the paper's reliability 0.8)'.
claims.note: All Morral numbers in the statement and magnitude were checked on rendered pages: NHSDA 1982 through 1994-A, 58,846 respondents aged 12-25, birth cohorts 1964-1982 (p. 1497); 157 vs 24 (p. 1500); 0.011 vs 0.016 (p. 1500), stated as 11 vs 16 per 1,000 people (p. 1501); OR 297 and 82 are printed data labels in Figure 4 (p. 1502), at reliabilities 0.0 and 0.8 read off the figure's axis (OR 2 at 0.99 is also in the text). No uncertainty interval is given for any model or survey estimate: confirmed. 'Not compared with a model that includes one' agrees with the authors' closing call for evidence comparing the gateway and common-factor models directly (p. 1503). Other points: the authors put the model's larger relative risk down to the tiny survey denominator (a 0.013 change could take the survey value above 190, p. 1500); younger vs older cannabis starters, survey 1.60 vs model 3.44 (p. 1500); the sentence defining order (p. 1500) uses Y_H < Y_M, the opportunity variables, where the initiation variables are meant (notational slip); the authors' policy inference that cannabis policies would have little effect on hard-drug use (p. 1503) goes further than showing that a no-effect model fits.

anchors.locator: Introduction, last paragraph; Methods > Model specification > Drug use propensity (continues on p. 1496)
anchors.extracted: Monte Carlo model of drug use initiation for US residents under 22: ages of first opportunity and first use of cannabis and of hard drugs all depend on one common propensity (drawn from a standard normal distribution) that raises both the chance of an opportunity at each age and the chance of use once offered; given propensity, cannabis opportunity and use are independent of hard-drug opportunity and use, so the model excludes any causal gateway effect by design.

anchors.locator: Methods > Parameter estimation > Data source (continues on p. 1498)
anchors.extracted: Parameters and observed comparison values from the NHSDA 1982 through 1994-A: 58,846 respondents aged 12-25 from birth cohorts 1964-1982, pooled and weighted; self-reported ages of first opportunity and first use; hard drugs = heroin, cocaine or hallucinogens.

anchors.locator: Model results > Gateway effects > Relative risk, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Model: by 21, people who had used cannabis were 157 times as likely as others to have started a hard drug; survey respondents aged 22 or older who had used cannabis by 21: 24 times. Authors attach little weight to the difference (small denominator; a 0.013 error could make the survey value above 190). Younger vs older cannabis starters: survey 1.60, model 3.44.

anchors.locator: Model results, 1st paragraph (begins p. 1499); Gateway effects > Ordering
anchors.extracted: Hard drugs counted as first only if started at least a year before cannabis and before 22 (ages in whole years). Proportion of simulated people starting hard drugs first 0.011 vs 0.016 in the survey.

anchors.locator: Discussion > Adolescent drug use initiation, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Order attributed to cannabis opportunities preceding hard-drug opportunities, often by years; model 11 per 1,000 people start hard drugs before cannabis vs 16 per 1,000 in the survey.

Hazard ratio for starting hard drugs rises with past-year cannabis frequency under all four assumed correlations (0, 0.4, 0.8, 1) between cannabis-use intensity and propensity; with zero correlation the most frequent group's hazard is more than 10 times that of no past-year use. Survey values (stars, read off the log-scale figure): about 7.5, 12, 23 and 40 for 1-2, 3-11, 12-51 and 52+ uses, near r = 0.4 at low frequencies and between 0.4 and 0.8 at the highest.

anchors.locator: Figure 4; Discussion > Exhibiting gateway effects by controlling for common factors, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 1501)
anchors.extracted: Logistic model of hard-drug initiation by 22 adjusted for a propensity indicator of given reliability: OR (data labels printed on the figure) 297 at reliability 0.0, 285 at 0.2, 245 at 0.4, 178 at 0.6, 82 at 0.8, 32 at 0.9, 12 at about 0.95, 2 at 0.99, 1 at 1.0 (reliabilities other than 0.99 read off the axis). Indicators must be almost perfectly correlated with propensity before the association disappears.

Untested assumptions (normal propensity, frailty model); the survey comparison values rest on assumptions too; parameters specific to US youth of that period; self-report bias could create the patterns, so propensity is defined as propensity to report use; the no-effect property holds whatever the parameter values. No intervals are given for any estimate.

anchors.locator: Discussion > The status of the marijuana gateway effect, 2nd and 4th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Authors think something like a gateway effect probably exists, if only because buying cannabis brings contact with a black market that also gives access to hard drugs; it could be tiny relative to propensity or offset by opposite effects in some people; they hold the gateway effect uncertain until evidence directly compares it with the common-factor model.
Each phenomenon cited for a gateway effect is reproduced by a model in which cannabis has no causal influence; gateway effects may exist but no gateway effect is required to explain the phenomena.

key_findings.note: Read off Figure 2 (p. 1498) at 300 dpi: proportions surviving at 22 about 0.23 (cannabis opportunity), 0.54 (hard-drug opportunity), 0.46 (cannabis initiation), 0.77 (hard-drug initiation); same as the card. Values read off a figure.
Editors' calculation recomputed: with 24 = p1/p0 and 190 = p1/(p0 - 0.013), p0 = 0.0149 and p1 = 0.357; the 0.013 the authors call slight is 87% of the survey denominator.

Figure 3 readings agree with mine (survey about 7.5, 12, 23, 40; zero-correlation model about 6, 8, 9, 12; read off the log-scale figure). Small precision: the paper calls its survey dose-response procedure inaccurate because frequency can change after hard-drug initiation in the same year (p. 1499); the proportional-hazards assumption is stated separately in that paragraph and listed as possibly wrong on p. 1502, not given as a reason for 'inaccurate'.
See reporting issue 4: the abscissa is the indicator's correlation with propensity.

reporting_issues.note: Checked on the 300 dpi render of p. 1496: equation 3 prints 0 for Y_M > t; and since S(t) = F(psi* - theta) S(t-1), F is the yearly probability of not starting, whereas the text after it equates E[F] with the probability of starting at t.
This bears on the claim's magnitude ('reliability 0.8' = correlation 0.8, 64% of variance); added to my claim note.

risk_of_bias.note: High overall on the editors' modelling checklist, mainly because no gateway model was fitted and the calibration targets only the margins. These concerns weigh on reading the model as the explanation of the data; they weigh much less on its narrower demonstration that the three phenomena can arise without any gateway effect, which is the only use the claim makes of it.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the statement that the phenomena can be explained completely (p. 1493) and the policy conclusion (p. 1503) go beyond a non-identification result, although the paper also says the gateway effect is not disproved and probably exists.

missed: The model results describe the relative risk as one for cases with and without earlier cannabis initiation (pp. 1499-1500), but the survey estimate it is compared with (24) counts cannabis use by 21 and hard-drug use by 21 regardless of order (p. 1499, Estimation of the relative risk effect); the two figures may not measure quite the same thing. Minor.
